morecompetitive examinations. fear, favour, &c. Every kingdom is under a greater kingdom. djevery kingdom lies under a heavier kingdom Source Probably Seneca, Thyestes, 612 (unverified)Notes The meaning is that every ruler is subject to a higher power. Seneca's line ends with 'est'; Burton leaves it out, which does not change the sense.
trans. in turn g
morein turn djin turn
Author trans. “justice equally done”
literalequal law
trans. … For who embraces virtue itself, / if you remove the reward? g
more— for who embraces virtue for its own sake, / if you take away its rewards? Source Probably Juvenal, Satires, 10.141–142 (unverified)
trans. whoever will strike the enemy will be a Carthaginian to me g
moreHe who shall slay an enemy shall be to me a Carthaginian djWhoever strikes the enemy shall be a Carthaginian to me Source Burton cites Ennius, Annales (unverified)Notes The line is preserved through Cicero, Pro Balbo, where the text reads 'mihi erit'.
trans. to indulge their appetites g
moreto indulge their humour, djto indulge their genius
A proverbial Latin phrase meaning to give oneself up to enjoyment and good cheer (the genius being a person's guardian spirit, the seat of appetite). Compare Persius, Satires 5, 'indulge genio'. trans. Sacred Festival dj
morefeast of the Sacaea Source Burton cites Athenaeus, lib. 14 (unverified)
The Sacaea was a Babylonian and Persian festival of misrule, in which masters and servants changed places, much like the Roman Saturnalia. Athenaeus describes it in book 14. Burton's form 'Saccarum' is irregular. trans. flogged in the amphitheatre g
moreflogged on the shoulders in the amphitheatre Source Burton cites Aelius Spartianus, Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian (unverified)
Catomidiare (from Greek kat' ōmōn, 'upon the shoulders') means to flog someone who is hoisted on another man's back. The phrase comes from the Historia Augusta's Life of Hadrian by Spartianus, where Hadrian orders bankrupts to be flogged this way in the amphitheatre. Burton's gloss 'publicly shamed' gives only the gist. trans. harsh law of the Persians g
morehard law of the Persians, djharsh law of the Persians Source Burton cites Barnabé Brisson (Brissonius), De regio Persarum principatu, Lib. 2 (unverified)Notes The law punished a whole family for one member's crime.
trans. those really terrifying and abominable laws by which, for the crime of a single man, all his relatives perish g
moreexceedingly dreadful and abominable laws, by which, for the offence of one man, his whole kindred perishes Source Burton cites Ammianus Marcellinus, Res gestae, Lib. 23 (unverified)Notes 'formiditas' is a corruption of 'formidatas' and 'omnius' of 'omnis'; the translation follows the corrected forms. Burton's English that follows gives the gist freely.
trans. except when there has been a dispensation to the contrary g
moreunless it is otherwise arranged. djunless a dispensation be granted to the contrary
trans. Extravagant funeral rites g
moreFuneral display djExtravagance at funerals Notes A sidenote in the same paragraph ("Idem Plato 12 de legibus, it hath ever been immoderate") points to Plato's limits on funeral expense in Laws 12. It supports the idea, not this phrase.

literalhere we are dealing with men, not with gods

literalif we were honest

moreWe say No, but 'tis but a word with ms, djWe deny it, but that word alone has been found, Notes This is a single verse line that breaks off with a comma. Its sense depends on a following line that is not given, so the rendering is tentative.
trans. per cent trans. overseers of the treasury g
moremanagers of the treasury djprefects of the treasury Notes Burton gives this Latin title as an alternative name for the 'supervisors'. It is the Roman name for officers of the public treasury.
trans. Prime Mover In Ptolemaic astronomy, the outermost sphere, whose daily revolution carries all the heavens with it and so provides a standard of measure. trans. for the safety of the people g
morefor the welfare of the people Notes This recalls the maxim 'salus populi suprema lex' ('the welfare of the people is the highest law').
trans. We hate the hawk, because it lives perpetually under arms, g
moreWe hate the hawk, because it lives forever in arms, Source Probably Ovid, Ars Amatoria, 2.147 (unverified)Notes This is the first line of a couplet; the second line, about wolves that prey on the timid flock, is not given. Standard texts seem to read 'quia vivit semper in armis'.
Author trans. “fair means shall first be tried”
literalAll things must be tried first
trans. Power accomplishes with peacefulness what it cannot by force g
morePowder exercised with moderation, can effect that w^hich violence could never accomplish. djCalm authority achieves what violent force cannot. Source Burton cites Claudian (unverified)
trans. for the man who relies on strategy hurts enemies more than someone who depends on force without calculation g
morefor he who relies on counsel does more harm to the enemy than he who relies on force without the reasoning of the mind Source Burton cites Thucydides (unverified)Notes The sidenote 'Thucydides.' stands in sequence at this point in the paragraph and probably belongs to this sentence, but this is not certain. Burton is contrasting Fabius, the cautious Roman general, with the rash Minucius.
trans. ready for action, and what Bonfinius wants with his Hungarians, a rod of iron g
moreBonfinius would have it among his Hungarians, an iron rod Source Burton cites Antonio Bonfini (Bonfinius), Rerum Hungaricarum decades, dec. 1 lib. 9 (unverified)Notes This continues the preceding '& quam' ('and, as'). The 'iron rod' seems to mean firm military discipline or a standing armed force always ready. The exact sense in Bonfinius is uncertain.
trans. the sinew of war g
morethe nerve of war, djthe sinew of war
A proverbial phrase for money. Cicero has a similar expression ('nervos belli, pecuniam'). trans. lest anything be done rashly, carelessly or timidly g
morebe done rashly, nothing slackly and timidly Notes This completes the 'ne quid' of the previous passage: 'that nothing be done rashly, nothing slackly and timidly.'
trans. but where am I hurrying, as an ignorant stranger? g
moreBut where am I being carried away to, friend? Notes 'Hospes' (guest, stranger) here addresses the reader. Burton uses the phrase to stop himself after a digression.
trans. Hands off the page g
moreBut hands off the picture! djHand off the picture
A proverb: know when to stop working. It goes back to the painter Apelles, who knew when to take his hand from the panel. Cicero also uses it. trans. in passing g
moreincidentally djin passing

literalluxury has squandered everything

literalnot without loss to hospitality

literalEven if Salvation herself were to desire it, she definitely couldn’t rescue this family g
trans. What tempest shakes this family? g
moreWhat madness vexes this family? djWhat madness troubles this family? Notes 'Intemperies' means a disordered state or distemper, here a fit of madness.
trans. thievish slaves, dissimulators, tricksters, they open doors with a thousand locks, they snatch furtively, they devour, they lick up g
moreslaves thievish, cunning, craft\^, such as open doors seal'd with a thousand keys, and stealthily snatch, and consume, and live on naught but dainties djthievish servants, shifty and crafty, who unlock what is shut against them with a thousand keys, and on the sly snatch, devour and lick it all up Notes Versipelles means 'skin-changers', so shifty or turncoat. The Plautine sidenotes in this paragraph ('Amphitheat. Plaut.', 'Plautus Aulular.') may refer to other phrases, so no source is given.
trans. what fools have recorded about fools g
morewhich fools have writ of fools, djwhich fools have written about fools
trans. It includes the rage of foolish kings and nations. g
moreIt holds the passions of foolish kings and peoples. Source Probably Horace, Epistles, 1.2.8 (unverified)
In Horace the line describes Homer's Iliad. Aestus means 'heats' or 'tides', that is, passionate turmoil. trans. … the kings commit madness, the Greeks are punished. g
moreWhen kings are mad, the people have to pay for't. dj— the kings rave, the Greeks are punished. Source Probably Horace, Epistles, 1.2.14 (unverified)
Horace's full line is 'quidquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi': whatever madness the kings commit, the Achaeans pay for it. Burton leaves out 'quidquid'. trans. far from Jupiter, far from the thunderbolt g
morefar from Jupiter, far from his thunderbolts, djfar from Jove, far from the thunderbolt Notes A proverb: the further you are from power, the safer you are.
trans. their temper stands and falls by his glance g
moretheir face, not merit, makes or mars their fortunes; djtheir spirit stands or falls by his countenance Notes Suo ('his') presumably refers to the prince, so the courtier's spirits rise and fall with the prince's looks. The line reads like Ovid, but it has not been securely identified.
trans. slaves of lust and folly g
moreslaves of lust and folly Source Burton cites Aeneas Silvius (Pius II), De miseriis curialium (unverified)
trans. the dictators of ancient wisdom g
moredictators of ancient wisdom

moreTo whom 'tis given to have brains a7td intellects, dj— to whom it has been given to have a sound mind / and to be 'little hearts' — Source Burton cites Janus Dousa, Epodes, lib. 1 car. 13 (unverified)Notes Corculum ('little heart') was a Roman surname of honour for men of great wisdom, since the heart was thought to be the seat of intelligence; Burton's second sidenote explains this. 'Wise souls' gives the sense.
trans. … Doctors, open up the median vein! g
moreO physicians, open the middle vein. dj— O physicians, lance the middle vein. Source Burton cites Juvenal, Satires (unverified)Notes The cure for madness is bloodletting from the median vein. 'Medici' and 'mediam' make a sound-play.
trans. could you restrain your laughter, my friends? g
more& " Could you keep from laughing, my friends djand could you keep from laughing, friends? Source Probably Horace, Ars Poetica, 5 (unverified)

The saying comes down through Seneca (On Tranquillity of Mind), who attributes it to Aristotle. trans. let the straight-legged man ridicule the bandy-legged, the white man ridicule the black g
moreLet the shapely man deride the bandy-legg'd, the white man the blackamoor. djLet the straight-legged mock the club-footed, the white man the Ethiopian Source Probably Juvenal, Satires, 2.23 (unverified)Notes Only someone free of the fault may mock it.
trans. solutions
moreNotes 'Obs and Sols' mocks the abbreviations used in scholastic disputation: ob. (objectio, objection) and sol. (solutio, solution). The phrase stands for the endless objections and answers of school divinity.
trans. incredible insanity g
moreincredible folly, djan incredible raving
trans. subtle Scotus, the polisher of truth, the irrefutable Occam, whose genius overthrew all the geniuses of the past, etc. g
moreScotus the file of truth, Occam the irrefragable, whose genius overturned all the geniuses of old, etc.
The marked span leaves out the preceding 'subtilis' ('the subtle'), which belongs with Scotus, the 'Subtle Doctor'. 'Irrefragabilis' was the usual scholastic title of Alexander of Hales; Occam was normally called 'Invincibilis' or the 'Venerable Inceptor'. Burton's attribution is translated as it stands. trans. the ‘Little Heart’ of Theology g
moreLittle Heart of Theology Notes A scholastic honorific. Corculum, 'little heart', also means 'darling' or 'sweetheart'. Which doctor Burton means by it is not certain.

morethey are too crazy for three Anticyras, dja head incurable by three Anticyras Source Probably Horace, Ars Poetica, 300 (unverified)
Anticyra was a town famous for hellebore, the classical cure for madness. Even three Anticyras' worth of the drug could not cure such a head. Author trans. “out of their volubility of tongue, will talk much to no purpose”
literalthey make a great stir to show off their talkativeness

morewhither they will, whence they will Notes The phrase recalls Cicero's praise of the orator's power to lead listeners wherever he likes, but the exact source is not certain.
trans. I prefer inarticulate wisdom to talkative stupidity g
moreI prefer silent Wisdom to talkative Folly; djI prefer wisdom that cannot speak well to folly that talks a great deal. Source Burton cites Cicero, De Oratore (unverified)Notes Cicero has 'malle ... indisertam prudentiam quam stultitiam loquacem', in indirect speech. Burton turns it into the first person.

moremad declaimers

moregives a voice without thought, djit gives out sound without mind Source Probably Virgil, Aeneid, 10.640 (unverified)
In Virgil the line describes the phantom of Aeneas that Juno fashions. Burton applies it to the nightingale and to the orator. trans. Either the man’s insane, or he’s making verses g

moregutters of folly, djthe dainties of absurdities Notes Ineptiae are trifles or absurdities. The scholars treat such trifles as dainties.

literalThey count themselves fools unless they can find something to fault in other men's writings

The full question is 'whether the egg or the hen came first'; the sidenote 'Macrob. Satur. 7. 16.' refers to it. In 'scire' the grammar is awkward. Seneca's wording is about things one would have to unlearn if one knew them.

moredung-hill reformers, djdunghills of correctors Source Burton cites Joseph Justus Scaliger, Lib. 2 in Ausonium, cap. 19 & 32 (unverified)Notes The sidenote 'Lib. 2 in Ausonium, cap. 19 & 32.' probably refers to Scaliger's notes on Ausonius.

literalthey spend their time for the most part among dung

morethe critic's treasure-house, djthe critical treasury Source Burton cites Janus Gruter (editor), Thesaurus criticus (unverified)Notes This is also the title of Janus Gruter's large collection of philological criticism, the Thesaurus criticus, published in several volumes; the sidenote points to it. Burton's 'before any treasure' plays on the title.

moredelete d; others read thus; my manuscript has it thus Notes Stock formulas from textual critics' notes.
trans. latest editions g
morelatest editions

literaleven Jupiter isn’t permitted to love and be wise at the same time g

morefoolish young lads Source Burton cites Cicero (unverified)

literalthen he began to be wise

literalw^ealth permits folly, dj

perhaps w gloss prentice An apprentice w gloss antic Grotesque, ludicrous.gloss personate Counterfeit, feigned.about Primum … coacturus est In the opening of Seneca’s satirical Pumpkinification of Claudius, quoted here, the narrator tells his readers that he has no obligation to divulge the source of his knowledge of the fantastical and absurd events that he is about to describe.note what was in it The answer given by an unidentified Egyptian is cited by Plutarch in On Being a Busybody (3) as an appropriate rebuke to someone who is inappropriately inquisitive into other people’s affairs – including the reader, who is told that ‘it would not be concealed, if it were not something bad’ (malum, in the Renaissance Latin translation by Guillaume Xylander which Burton probably used, also carries the senses of ‘mischievous’, ‘harmful’, ‘inappropriate’ and ‘insulting’).note pasquil Lampoon; see also below, .gloss paradox A barely believable or strange doctrine.about Praxiteles A celebrated Athenian sculptor of the fourth century BCE.about Mercurius Gallobelgicus The title of a contemporary Latin newsletter printed in Germany and circulating in England.about Mercurius Britannicus The pseudonym used by the English bishop and writer Joseph Hall in his satirical Mundus alter et idem (1605).about Democritus Christianus The title of the 1616 Latin version of Le Démocrite chrestien (1615) by the French cardinal, bishop and author Pierre de Besse.gloss wearish Wizened, shrivelled.gloss Physician Natural philosopher.about Politician An expert in the theory of politics.note liberales disciplinas In note ‘l’, the ‘liberal sciences’ – often called the ‘liberal arts’ – were the seven disciplines traced to antiquity and taught in the universities (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy).about Recorder Someone employed to record civil documents (or, in its original meaning, a magistrate or judge).gloss reference Submission to a higher authority.source Xenocrates in Athens According to Diogenes Laertius (4.2), the philosopher Xenocrates (b. 396/5 BCE) served as head of the Platonic Academy in Athens for twenty-five years, until his death at the age of eighty-two.about Otho Nicholson In note ‘g’, Otho Nicholson (d. 1622) was a wealthy London lawyer and one of James I’s Examiners in Chancery. He paid for the restoration of the library building at Christ Church in 1610–11, and gave a donation of money for the purchasing of books in 1613.gloss Card Plan, or chart.note Saturn was Lord of my geniture … in their houses, &c. In astrology, the ‘lord of the geniture’ was whichever planet was the dominant influence at the time of a person’s nativity. Burton refers here to his horoscope, a copy of which (drawn up in his own hand) is found in one of his books now held in the Bodleian Library, and reproduced on his monument in the cathedral of Christ Church in Oxford. It shows that at his birth (8 February 1577), Saturn was at the highest point in the sky and in the sign of Capricorn, and that the ‘ascendant’ (the sign rising on the eastern horizon) was Aries, one of the ‘houses’ (the twelve parts of the zodiac with particular significance in human affairs) which was ruled and at that point occupied by Mars. The putatively malign influences of Saturn and Mars were thereby thought to be tempered – and hence were ‘fortunate in their houses’.source garden From the third edition (1628) onwards, this passage replaced the following in the earlier versions: ‘although my friends’ providence, care, alacrity, and bounty was never wanting to do me good, yet either through mine own default, infelicity, want or neglect of opportunity, iniquity of times, preposterous proceeding, my hopes were still frustrate, and I left behind, as a Dolphin on shore, confined to my College, as Democritus to his garden, Diogenes to his tub, where I still continue’. In this passage, ‘default’ means ‘defect’ or ‘failure’. The ancient Greek philosopher Diogenes the Cynic is said to have slept in a large ceramic wine-jar – often referred to as a ‘barrel’ or ‘tub’ – exemplifying his scornful rejection of social convention, and contributing to his reputation, as Plato is reported to have said, as a ‘Socrates gone mad’.gloss macerate Weaken, vex.gloss only Uniquely, pre-eminently.gloss spectrums Phantoms, spectres.gloss monomachies Duels.gloss corantoes Newsletters or newspapers.gloss fashions Manners and customs.gloss several Different.note day net A net that can be suddenly pulled shut, used in the hunting of larks and other small birds.gloss passengers Passers-by.gloss conceited Ingenious, clever.gloss except against Object, protest.note genius The Latin term can refer to a tutelary spirit or deity (good or evil), but also, and sometimes simultaneously, to the innate character or nature of a person.gloss impostume A swelling or abscess, thought to be caused by the superfluity of a humour.gloss offended Harmed, hurt.about Aegeria Or Egeria: in Roman mythology, a water-goddess and one of the prophetic nymphs known as the Camenae (later identified with the inspirational Muses of Greek mythology). Egeria was said to have acted as counsellor to the second legendary king of Rome, Numa Pompilius, and was associated with wisdom and oracular inspiration.note private Intimate (or here, perhaps, discreet and dependable). In note ‘d’, the named individuals refer to contemporaries of Burton at Oxford: Rous was the Head Librarian (‘Protobibliothecarius’) of the Bodleian Library; Thomas Hopper and John Goodridge (‘Guthridge’) bequeathed many medical books to their colleges.source myself The quotation, adapted slightly from Sallust’s War with Jugurtha (85.13), is from the speech of the Roman general and politician Gaius Marius (157–86 BCE), delivered to his forces in 107 before they leave to fight the Numidian king in North Africa.gloss just Full, complete.gloss disparagement Degradation.note divine, humane authors Writers on divinity and the ‘humanities’ – the classically orientated studia humanitatis of poetry, rhetoric, grammar, history and moral philosophy.gloss set out Adorn, decorate.about Trium literarum homines In Plautus’ Pot of Gold (325), the ‘trium litterarum homo’ is the man of the three letters f, u and r, spelling ‘thief’ in Latin.gloss putid Worthless or foul.gloss close-stool An enclosed cabinet containing a chamber pot.gloss jakes Latrine.gloss lap Wrap up.gloss vilified Reduced in value or estimation.gloss collogue Coax, blandish.gloss vent their toys Sell their trifling writings.about Sossius Sinesius Actually (Quintus) Sosius Senecio, a Roman senator (and consul in 99 and 107 CE).note our Frankfurt Marts, our domestic Marts The Frankfurt book fair, which was the most important of its kind in early modern Europe and was held twice a year, was far larger than the book fairs in contemporary England.about Chaos The ‘formless void’ of primordial matter out of which the earth was made.about Maceronicon A literary work composed of two or more languages; alternatively, a jumble or medley.gloss likely Similarly.gloss indite Express or dictate words for a literary composition.gloss solve Answer.gloss Doric dialect Unrefined speech.gloss rhapsody A work made up of miscellaneous elements without fixed form, a literary hodge-podge.gloss insolent Bizarre.gloss indiscreet Or ‘undiscreet’ – undiscerning.note parasangs An ancient Persian unit of length: the distance travelled in one hour (whether by foot or horseback, however, is uncertain), and usually thought to be approximately 3¾ miles.gloss ace A particle, or the smallest amount possible.gloss bewrays Exposes, betrays.source old Cato’s rule This was actually the belief of Plutarch, expressed in his biography of Cato the Elder (7.2) – for whom, see above, .gloss another According to a classical adage, marjoram is repulsive to pigs.gloss strong lines Obscure or bombastic writing.note the Dominicals Engravings illustrating the contemplative devotions; they were modelled on places and events taken from the ‘Dominical’ (Sunday) Gospel readings, and included in the Adnotationes et meditationes in Evangelia (1595), a spiritual manual compiled by the Spanish Jesuit Jérôme Nadal (Natalis).gloss explodes Rejects or condemns.gloss trivant A lazy person; or, more strongly, an idle rogue.gloss brave Fine, splendid.gloss doctor An eminently learned person.gloss Dutch German.gloss witty Wise, ingenious.gloss painful Diligent, painstaking.source Arena sine calce The quotation from Suetonius (Gaius Caligula 53) in note ‘b’ refers to the quicklime required to make mortar.gloss propugner Advocate, champion.gloss absolute Perfect.gloss prescription Ancient or continued custom.gloss take place Have effect.gloss advice Reflection, deliberation (here, probably without the assistance of another).note doth her young ones A reference to the ancient belief that newborn bears are not fully formed, but are ‘licked into shape’ by their mothers.gloss fustian Inflated or inappropriately lofty in expression.source Acestes’ arrows … flew An allusion to the archery competition in the Aeneid (5.519–40), won by Acestes (Virgil’s name for Aegestus, the son of Trojan parents who had fled to Sicily) when his arrow burst into flames to indicate his divine favour.gloss strains of wit Strained literary constructions (or, alternatively, streams of affective language).gloss brave heats Expressions of intense feeling.gloss elogies Eulogies.gloss exornations Decorations, adornments.source Apollonius, a scholar of Socrates Apollonius of Tyana (first century CE), a Neopythagorean holy man; ‘scholar’ here means ‘pupil’. According to Philostratus (Life of Apollonius of Tyana 8.2), if called to defend himself in court, Apollonius would have imitated the succinct and apposite speech given by Socrates at his trial.note here champian, there enclosed Or, ‘here free and open, there constrained’. A ‘champian’ (or ‘champaign’) was an open and level plain, whereas ‘enclosed’ land had been converted from common ownership into private property.note ut canis Nilum lambens In note ‘d’, ‘like a dog lapping at the Nile’ is a standard trope for dabbling, deriving from the ancient observation that dogs would not stay by the water of that river for any length of time because of its crocodiles.gloss censure Judgement, opinion.gloss pleonasms Superfluities, redundancies.gloss interpretations Direct or literal translations.gloss margent Margin.gloss interpreters Translators.gloss Neoterics Modern authors.about I have done This resolution first appeared in the third edition (1628). It remained in, and did not prevent, the editions issued in 1632, 1638 and 1651.about Chremes Two Athenian characters in Terence’s Self-Tormentor.gloss deboshed Debauched.gloss rillet A rivulet or stream.note positively Dogmatically, or engaging in a controversy. Paul’s Cross … St.about Mary’s Oxon Two locations where sermons were commonly preached: the pulpit cross at St Paul’s Cathedral in London and the University Church of St Mary’s in Oxford.note to cut off an Hydra’s head In classical mythology, when each of the multiple heads of the Hydra were cut off, two more grew back in its place.note duplications, triplications In law, the ‘duplication’ is the defendant’s reply to the ‘replication’ (a claimant’s answer to a defendant’s plea), and the ‘triplication’ is the plaintiff’s reply to the defendant’s duplication.gloss irrefragable Obstinate, inflexible.gloss sciences Branches of learning.source de lana caprina A proverbially trivial dispute (referred to in Horace, Epistles 1.18.15) about whether goat’s hair can be called ‘wool’.gloss about moonshine in the water Proverbially, about nothing.about Drusianus The learned Italian physician Pietro Torrigiano de’ Torrigiani (d. c. 1319), whose name was Latinized variously as ‘Turisanus’, ‘Trusianus’ or ‘Drusianus’.about Linacre The English humanist scholar and physician Thomas Linacre (c. 1460–1524).about Chirurgeons Surgeons – in the early modern era, medical practitioners who treated diseases or injuries manually.gloss driven to their shifts Pushed to the last extremity, to the point of extreme difficulty or ‘last resort’.note mountebanks, quacksalvers, empirics Types of physician generally regarded by the learned medical community as spurious. ‘Mountebanks’ were itinerant charlatans selling remedies; ‘quacksalvers’ were untrained doctors or ‘quacks’; and ‘empirics’ were untrained doctors who, unlike learned physicians, treated diseases without theoretical knowledge of their causes (the term derives from the ancient medical sect of the Empirici, who drew their rules entirely from experience).note taskers Labourers who work or are paid by the task or piece (as distinct from day-labourers).gloss costermongers Apple- or fruit-sellers.gloss graziers People who graze or feed cattle for the market.gloss prospectives Scenes or views drawn in perspective.gloss chorographical Describing, or delineating on a map or chart, a particular region or district.about Jupiter in my sixth house An indication of suitability for the medical profession, according to some Renaissance astrologers.gloss theoric Theory.gloss humanity Or the ‘humanities’: see above, .about to reconcile those Chronological errors in the Assyrian monarchy A reference to recent chronological disputes about the reigns of the Assyrian kings, which – as the classical scholar Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) had pointed out – were difficult to reconcile with the accounts given in Scripture.note find out the quadrature of a circle The geometrical process of constructing a square equal in area to that of a circle.note the north-east, or north-west passages Supposed short, direct routes to China and India through the northern polar regions, searched for by explorers such as Henry Hudson (d. 1611) – see below, .about that hungry Spaniard’s … Terra Australis Incognita In 1603, the Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós (1563–1615) had been commissioned by Philip III of Spain to discover ‘the Unknown Southern Continent’ (the mythical terra australis), which had been the subject of speculation since antiquity, and was often seen in the early modern period as a second ‘new world’ to be explored and colonized.about perfect the motion of Mars and Mercury The elliptical orbits of these two planets had been established in 1609 by the astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), who had elaborated them further in 1619.note rectify the Gregorian Calendar The Gregorian calendar was introduced in Catholic Europe in 1582, but the continued adherence to the Julian calendar in Protestant states (until 1752 in the case of England) led to conflicts over the dating of events in the ecclesiastical year.about that great captain Zisca The Bohemian general Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424), a Hussite – that is, a follower of the ecclesiastical reformer Jan Hus (1372–1415) – who led his army to several victories even after he had become completely blind in 1421.note to their benefit This warning first appeared in the third edition of 1628, and it remained in the editions of 1632, 1638 and 1651.gloss gulls Credulous or gullible people, fools.about Morea may be Moria The Peloponnese was known as ‘Morea’ in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. In Greek, as Erasmus had remarked to Thomas More in the preface to the Moriae encomium (1511), μωρία means ‘folly’.note vegetal, sensible, and rational See below, 1.1.2.5; ‘sensible’ creatures are those endowed with sense-perception.about Cebes’ table The Tablet (Pinax) then falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Cebes of Thebes (c. 430–350 BCE), which allegorically represents the correct and false paths in life.gloss actions Legal processes or speeches.about Porcius Latro Marcus Porcius Latro (c. 55–4 BCE), a famously forceful Roman rhetorician, given the last declamation in the Controversies (a set of fictional legal debates) of Seneca the Elder (c. 55 BCE–39/40 CE).gloss confound Mix up, confuse.note the Anticyrae The plural form refers to the fact that there were three towns named Anticyra in ancient Greece; one of these, a Phocian port on the bay of Anticyra in the Gulf of Corinth, was renowned for its black hellebore, a famous remedy for madness and melancholy.note Compostella, our Lady of Sichem, or Lauretta Santiago de Compostela in Spain, Zichem in the Low Countries and Loreto in Italy, all renowned destinations for Catholic pilgrims and those in search of miraculous cures.note a voyage … of Tobacco There had been several English attempts to colonize Guiana (in what is now Venezuela) in the reigns of Elizabeth I and James I. The region was noted for its abundance of sugar and tobacco.source Agur the son of Jakeh According to Proverbs 30:1, the author of this chapter of Scripture. The preceding chapters are ascribed to Solomon.note Quis nisi mentis inops, &c. In note ‘a’, the line being quoted – from the epic poet and theologian Walter of Châtillon (d. c. 1204) – in full is ‘Quis nisi mentis inops oblatum respuat aurum’: ‘Who but the mindless would refuse the offer of gold?’source Apollo According to Plato, the oracle at the temple of Apollo (the Greek god of divination, healing and music, among other things) at Delphi had proclaimed that no one was wiser than Socrates.about Brasidas The Spartan general (d. 422 BCE), who rose to prominence in the Peloponnesian War (431–404), was regarded as a model of bravery.about Antenor and Nestor In classical mythology, two elderly counsellors highly respected for their wisdom, on opposite sides – the Trojan and Greek respectively – during the Trojan War.about Pericles the statesman, orator and general (495–429), portrayed by Thucydides as the patriotic leader of the Athenian democracy in the 430s.about viris pueri The ancient Greek sophists Protagoras of Abdera (c. 490–420 BCE) and Gorgias of Leontini (c. 485–c. 380 BCE) had been influentially criticized by Plato in dialogues named after them – the former for his doctrine that ‘Man is the measure of all things’, the latter for his prioritization of rhetoric over philosophy. In the place cited here, Aelian contrasts them unfavourably with Democritus and the Pythagorean philosopher Philolaus (c. 470–390 BCE).gloss in respect In comparison.note as he censured Alexander In The History of the World (1614), Sir Walter Ralegh claimed that Alexander the Great ‘had ten thousand in his Army as daring as himself’.gloss dizzards Idiots, blockheads.about Aristippus Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 430–355 BCE), a student of Socrates, and sometimes seen as a bon viveur.note saved him from the plague Socrates escaped the plague that ravaged Athens in 430 BCE.note his Master His superior. Aristotle was generally regarded as the most accomplished ancient philosopher by Renaissance scholars, although Plato or Socrates were sometimes preferred.gloss opinative Opinionated.note so convict by Anytus That is, ‘proved to be so’ by Anytus, the Athenian politician who, together with Meletus, prosecuted Socrates at the latter’s trial for impiety and corrupting the young in 399 BCE.about Zenodotus’ heart, Crates’ liver Zenodotus (c. 325–260 BCE) and Crates of Mallus (fl. second century BCE) were Greek grammarians and scholars of Homer. In the epigram by the Roman poet Marcus Furius Bibaculus (b. 103 BCE) alluded to here, the heart and the liver both represent the physical seat of the intelligence, although the liver was more typically associated with the emotions.about Epictetus’ lantern In a story told in Lucian’s Ignorant Book-Collector (13), a man buys the lantern of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus in the hope of sharing his wisdom.about Crassians Literally, followers of the Crassus family in ancient Rome, but the term ‘Crassian’ had acquired a double meaning from the meaning of crassus in Latin as ‘thick’ or ‘stupid’. The ancient Roman cognomen ‘Crassus’, which was used in the republican period by several important families (most notably the plebeian Licinii Crassi), had initially been used as an epithet for unusual tallness.note two-legged asses In the Metamorphoses (sometimes called the Golden Ass), the ancient Numidian writer Apuleius (b. c. 125 CE) portrays the transformation of its narrator Lucius, identified in the final book as the author himself, into an ass.note inversorum Silenorum In classical mythology, a Silenus (or satyr) was a demonic inhabitant of the wild, combining human and animal characteristics, and associated with grotesque hedonism and the god Dionysus (Bacchus); ‘Silenus’ as a singular figure referred to the father or grandfather of the Silenuses/satyrs, also the foster-father and companion of Dionysus, and was traditionally depicted as an old, pot-bellied man. The allusion here, however, derives more specifically from Plato’s Symposium (215B, 216D, 221E), where Alcibiades describes a Silenus as a statue of a satyr containing the image of a god, and then compares one to Socrates – meaning that the philosopher’s external ugliness is belied by his inner beauty and wisdom. An ‘inverted Silenus’ therefore denotes external beauty and inner deformity.gloss fond Foolish, silly.gloss babies of clouts Rag dolls (‘dolls made of rags’).gloss get a head Gain power or ascendancy, become established.gloss promiscuous Mixed and disorderly.gloss emmets Ants.source Thersites According to Homer (Iliad 2.211–77), a lame, abusive and exceedingly ugly Greek soldier in the Trojan War.gloss swell Become ‘puffed up’ or arrogant.gloss molestation Affliction, vexation.gloss conversation Behaviour, mode of living.about Maecenas In note ‘a’, Gaius Cilnius Maecenas (d. 8 BCE) was the patron of Horace and Virgil, and a famously wealthy lover of luxury.gloss prank up Dress ostentatiously, decorate.gloss fleer Laugh at mockingly, ridicule.gloss Apologues Moral fables, usually allegorical.note whifflers Originally attendants employed to clear the way for a procession, but figuratively, swaggerers or bullies.about Cuman asses Fools whose novelties are taken to be signs of talent. The phrase refers to the classical fable of the ass which deceived the inhabitants of Cumae by wearing a lion-skin.gloss outsides Empty or superficial people.about Jupiter & Juno’s wedding Jupiter, the sovereign god of the Romans (and the equivalent of the Greek Zeus), was married to Juno (Hera), the goddess of women and marriage (as well as an important civic deity throughout central Italy).about Pluto The Roman god of the dead and king of the underworld (the counterpart of the Greek Hades).about Moronia Pia, and Moronia Foelix In Joseph Hall’s Mundus alter et idem (1605), the country of ‘Moronia’ (the land of fools, or ‘Fooliana’ in John Healey’s seventeenth-century English translation) contained the regions ‘Moronia Pia’ (‘Fooliana the Devout’), populated by religious heretics and the superstitious, and ‘Moronia Felix’ (‘Fooliana the Fat’), containing the proud and boastful.source be worst The prophecy of Jesus (recorded in Matthew 12:45) about the ‘wicked generation’ possessed by evil spirits.about Father Angelo … to Rome, &c. Note ‘g’ refers to a famous pilgrimage made by Henri, duke of Joyeuse (1563–1608), a Catholic general in the French Wars of Religion (1562–98) who had become a Capuchin, and taken the name ‘Frère Ange’, after the death of his wife.see to tread on Emperors’ necks … stirrup See below, .gloss beads Prayers or devotions conducted with rosary beads.note hallowed beans Possibly a reference to the Catholic practice of eating beans at Lent, sometimes associated with the commemoration of the dead.note the Golden Legend The Aurea legenda, or Legenda sanctorum, a collection of hagiographies compiled in the second half of the thirteenth century by the Italian chronicler and archbishop of Genoa, Jacopo da Voragine (1228/9–98).note the Turks’ Alcoran The Qur’an.about Rabbins’ Comments Rabbinical commentaries on the Torah or Talmud.note supererogate Earn merit for others by doing more than is required by God.note nice & curious schismatics Both ‘nice’ and ‘curious’ here mean ‘fastidious’, or ‘exceedingly careful and precise’ – qualities often derogatorily attributed to contemporary puritans, who are also the ‘schismatics’ being accused here of destroying the unity of the English Church.gloss things indifferent Matters that are non-essential to salvation.gloss lying at lurch Lying in wait, lurking.about Formalists People who adhere only outwardly to religious orthodoxy.gloss gripers ‘Graspers’ or extortioners.gloss greenheads Inexperienced, immature people.about Mahomet the second Turk The Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (1432–81), also known as Mehmed the Conqueror, whose military expansion of the Ottoman Empire led to his portrayal as a murderous tyrant in many Christian sources.about Sicinius Dentatus Lucius Siccius (or Sicinius) Dentatus (d. 450/49 BCE), a plebeian military hero later called ‘the Roman Achilles’. M.about Sergius The Roman general – and great-grandfather of Catiline: see below, – Marcus Sergius Silus, famous for his service in several campaigns in the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE).about Scaeva the Centurion Marcus Cassius Scaeva, who fought in the army of Julius Caesar in the Roman civil wars and distinguished himself in the siege of Dyrrachium (48 BCE).about Cannae The victory of Hannibal at the Battle of Cannae (216 BCE), during the Second Punic War, was one of Rome’s bloodiest and most ignominious defeats.about Battle Abbey The Battle of Hastings (1066), commemorated in the building of Battle Abbey.about as Constantine and Licinius The Roman emperors Licinius (c. 250–324 CE) and Constantine I (c. 275–337 CE) were initially allies and co-emperors, but became hostile rivals; the allusion here is probably to their struggle at the Battle of Cibalae in 314.about the siege of Ostend The city of Ostend, at the time occupied by Dutch and English troops, was besieged by Spanish forces between July 1601 and September 1604, during the Dutch Revolt (1568–1648).gloss dorps Villages.about mine Author Here, the French historian and bookseller Jérémie Périer (fl. 1588–1624).gloss condoles Laments.note that immortal Genius Fame.about the top of the walls The Ottoman Sultan (‘great Turk’) Suleiman I, commonly known as Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566), took Rhodes after a five-month siege in 1522, but his siege of Vienna in 1529 was unsuccessful.about Hectorem In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of the Trojan prince Hector. After the fall of Troy she became the slave and concubine of Neoptolemus (or Pyrrhus), the son of Achilles and a warrior infamous for his brutality in the sack of the city.about Collignius Gaspard II de Coligny (1519–72), a Huguenot leader in the French Wars of Religion (1562–98), who was himself killed in the St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre in Paris in August 1572.about Pharsalian fields Julius Caesar defeated his rival Pompey the Great at the Battle of Pharsalus in Thessaly (48 BCE). Here the phrase is used to signify the carnage of civil war, specifically at the Battle of Towton (1461) during the Wars of the Roses in England.gloss immanity Monstrous cruelty.gloss stupend Stupendous, amazing.note stone In classical mythology, Niobe’s grieving and transformation into stone occurs after her children are killed by Apollo and Artemis (Diana), as a punishment for her boasting about having more children than their mother Leto (Latona).about those fantastical Anabaptists Protestant sects, originating in Switzerland but spreading to Germany, the Low Countries and England in the early Reformation, who shared the belief that since infant baptism was not authorized by Scripture it should only be performed in adulthood. Their millenarian tendencies, rejection of traditional religious authority, emphasis on the community of believers, and belief in personal revelation – all crystallized in the notorious communal theocracy briefly established by John of Leiden at Münster (1534–5) – led to their widespread association with religious heterodoxy, social unrest and political radicalism.note the Roman Acies The Roman military term for the front of an army or a line of battle; or figuratively, the whole army drawn up in order of battle.about Calgacus’… in Tacitus Calgacus was one of the leaders of the Caledonian tribes who fought the Romans at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly north of Aberdeen) in 84 CE.gloss caitiffs Miserable people, poor wretches.gloss generous Brave, or noble.note lie sentinel perdue To be placed as a far-lying outpost or scout (and so to be in a position of extreme danger).gloss battle Battle array, an army or battalion in array.source when Darius’ army … Alexander at Issus According to the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus, before the Persian king Darius III was defeated at the Battle of Issus (333 BCE) he was warned by an Athenian adviser that his splendidly equipped army would prove no match for the well-disciplined forces of Alexander the Great.note proletaries Proletarians: the lowest class of citizens (in ancient Rome, those who owned little or no property), or the poor.about Plataea Famous battles in the Graeco-Persian Wars, fought between alliances of the Greek city-states against the Persian Empire in the fifth centuryabout Mantinea The site of three important battles, in 418, 362 and 207, but the reference here is probably to the second of these, fought between the Thebans and the Spartans.about Chaeronaea The site of the decisive victory, in 338, of Philip of Macedon over Athens, Thebes and their allies.about Ennius The victory of the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus (the Elder) (236–183 BCE) over Carthage in the Second Punic War (218–201) was commemorated in a poem traditionally attributed to the venerated Latin writer Quintus Ennius (239–169), although the authorship of the Scipio is now disputed.gloss feral Deadly.gloss for ‘On account of’ (or possibly ‘before’, ‘in front of’).gloss event Outcome.note pill and poll Literally, ‘remove the skin and hair’ – and so, figuratively, strip bare by pillage, plunder.gloss turgent Swollen or inflated with pride or conceit.gloss funge Someone who is ‘soft-headed’, like a mushroom or fungus.note fumes Insubstantial, transient or imaginary things – here, words, and possibly with the implication that they ‘go to the head’ and cloud the mental faculties or the reason.note a Gorgon’s head A very ugly person.note coats Petticoats or skirts (as worn in this period by young boys as well as girls).gloss made Prepared.gloss nose of wax Something easily twisted or moulded – and so here a person easily influenced.note firm in his opinion, cast in his That is, supported by one judge and ruled against by another.source punished ‘Silly’ here means helpless and innocent, corresponding loosely to the ‘doves’ in the line from Juvenal (Satires 2.63) partially quoted in note ‘f’ (‘It acquits the ravens and persecutes the doves’).about As put case To put the case, suppose.gloss policy Art or practice of government, conduct of public affairs.gloss compendious Sparing of time, or economical.gloss commodity Self-interest.source Eia Socrates, Eia Xantippe According to Diogenes Laertius (2.5), Socrates imagined his friends encouraging him to fight in the marketplace with his wife Xanthippe, who is traditionally portrayed as a shrew.source lacerant A quotation from Petronius’ Satyricon (116), where Croton (referred to in note ‘f’, now Crotone in Calabria) is depicted as an uncultured and corrupt city, once powerful and flourishing but now dominated by unscrupulous legacy hunters.about Vatinian hatred The Roman politician Publius Vatinius (b. c. 95 BCE) was publicly attacked in 56 by Cicero, who was then his declared political enemy. Although Vatinius was elected consul in 47, Cicero’s speeches led to his later becoming a proverbial object of intense animosity.gloss bestead Assist or relieve.about Cato … an old servant In fact, Cato the Elder was criticized by Plutarch for mistreating his slaves in precisely this manner.about Bajazet … make him away Sultan Bayezid II (1447–1512) had his admiral Gedik Ahmed Pasha executed in 1482 (‘Bassa’ is a variant spelling of ‘bashaw’, itself an earlier form of the title ‘Pasha’).note as Silius … Tiberius The Roman senator and general Gaius Silius was forced by the emperor Tiberius (42 BCE–37 CE) to commit suicide in 24 CE, after claiming that without his help the mutinous Roman legions on the Rhine would have removed the latter from power.about Dea moneta ‘Moneta’ was one of the epithets of Juno. The Romans had a temple on the Capitoline Hill dedicated to Juno Moneta, probably because of its proximity to the mint.gloss depressed Lowered, or kept down.source Prima fere … &c. The full quotation from Juvenal (Satires 10.23–4) in note ‘f’ is given below, p. 684 (3.1.2.1).gloss cogging Cheating, wheedling.source vivunt The quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.3) in note ‘c’ refers to the gens Curia, a Roman plebeian family associated with traditional virtue principally because of the reputation of Manius Curius Dentatus, censor in 272 BCE, for incorruptibility and modesty.gloss ambidexters Double-dealers, practising on both sides.gloss turning pictures Pictures which show different images when seen from different angles.about Proteus In classical mythology, a minor sea-god with shape-shifting qualities.note like Mercury the Planet In Renaissance astrology, the influence of Mercury was thought to oscillate between benevolence and malevolence, depending on its relationship with other planets.gloss garb Demeanour.gloss baffled Disgraced, treated with contempt.note glass In note ‘h’, a ‘perspective glass’ is a magnifying glass, telescope, or optical instrument devised to produce unusual visual effects.gloss livor Ill-will, spite.gloss jade An ill-tempered, worn-out or worthless horse.gloss pined Starved, tormented.about Alphonsus King Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458).source fortune’s fan turns ‘Fan’ probably means ‘vane’ or ‘weathercock’, although contemporary poetic usage of the phrase ‘fortune’s fan’ suggests that it could refer to a tool for winnowing grain (via allusion to Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17, where John the Baptist predicts the coming of Jesus as one ‘[w]hose fan is in his hand, and he will th[o]roughly purge his floor’).note an hundred oaks on his back That is, wearing expensive clothing purchased with the proceeds from the sale of a large quantity of land.gloss Anthropophagi Cannibals (literally, ‘human-eaters’).gloss genius Here, appetite.note ruffle Brag or swagger. The 1632 edition has ‘russle’ (‘rustle’).gloss obligation In law, a written contract or bond.note paint Thais Thais was a famous Athenian courtesan of the fourth century BCE, and was allegedly a mistress of Alexander the Great and subsequently of the Egyptian king Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367/6–282 BCE), but her name here is being used figuratively to refer to any courtesan; ‘paint’ here means ‘adorn with colours’, that is, by applying cosmetics.gloss philologer A literary scholar.about Aesop’s ape In the fable ‘Jupiter and the Monkey’, a mother ape is ridiculed when she presents her ugly offspring as the most beautiful beast in the forest.gloss wittol A contented cuckold, a fool.gloss colon Farmer.gloss moil Work hard, drudge.gloss insist in Dwell at length upon.about Vulcan’s man In Lucian’s Hermotimus, or Concerning the Sects (20), the figure of Momus criticizes the design of man by Hephaestus for lacking a means of easily discerning ‘his thoughts and designs, his truth or falsehood’. Hephaestus was the Greek god of fire, blacksmiths and artisans, and the equivalent of the Roman god Vulcan; he was traditionally associated with the creation of Pandora, the goddess of the earth (and the cause of all human miseries), and it is Lucian’s witty extrapolation to give him this role for mankind. On Momus, see above, .about Gallus The Latin term for a cockerel, and the eponymous character in Lucian’s dialogue.about Gyges’ invisible ring In classical mythology, King Gyges of Lydia (seventh century BCE) had been a shepherd who rose to power by using a magic ring that rendered its wearer invisible.about Otacousticon An ear trumpet, or a similar instrument to assist hearing.note species The bearers of sense-data – see the account of ‘sensible species’ at 1.1.2.7, and below.gloss projectors Schemers.source Seneca’s blind woman Harpaste, the female clown in the household of Seneca, who reports that she went blind without realizing it (Epistles 50.2–3).source Clodius accusat moechos The quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.27) in note ‘a’ refers to the notoriously dissolute Roman politician Publius Clodius Pulcher (c. 93–52 BCE).note his own spouse The reference is taken from Cicero’s letters to his friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, but the passage is actually a quotation of the Roman poet Atilius (second century CE).note take himself by the nose That is, ‘take a look at yourself’ (following the medieval proverb, ‘Accipe per nasum te, cum me dicis iniquam’: ‘If you call me harsh, take yourself by the nose’).note as Marsyas was … Apollo In classical mythology, the satyr Marsyas was flayed alive after challenging Apollo to a musical contest.note a most grievous poller himself Before turning to history-writing, Sallust (86–35 BCE) faced charges of exploiting the Roman province of Africa Nova (Numidia), of which he had been the first governor; ‘poller’ here means ‘despoiler’ or ‘plunderer’.about as mad as himself In his speech In Defence of Sextus Roscius of Ameria, Cicero presents the politician Gaius Flavius Fimbria (consul in 104 BCE) as an insane criminal, underlining the audacity of his attempted assassination (and then attempted prosecution) of the eminent lawyer and statesman Quintus Mucius Scaevola (c. 140–82 BCE); and see below, .gloss jangling Babbling or squabbling.note a hog still Drawing on the tenth book of the Odyssey, in which the companions of Odysseus (Ulysses) were transformed by Circe into animals, Plutarch’s Gryllus describes Odysseus’ attempt to restore them to human form, and relates the argument of Gryllus (now a pig) that animals have greater virtue and intelligence than humans. Elpenor, the youngest companion of Odysseus, is not mentioned in the dialogue.gloss bray Pound, crush to powder.about Athamas In classical mythology, the king of Orchomenus in Boeotia driven mad by one of the Furies (Tisiphone), sent by Hera (Juno) out of jealousy because he and his wife Ino had brought up the child Dionysus, the son of Zeus (Jupiter).gloss good parts Good qualities.note seven wise men The ‘Seven Sages’ of the early sixth century BCE reputed to have outstanding practical and political wisdom, traditionally Thales of Miletus, Bias of Priene, Cleobulus of Lindus (on Rhodes), Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Chilon of Sparta and Periander of Corinth (sometimes replaced by Myson of Chen, Anacharsis or others).source Thales sent the golden Tripos … to Solon, &c. In the traditional story (Diogenes Laertius 1.27), a group of fishermen discovered a golden tripod in the water, and after arguments about its ownership it was determined that the matter should be settled by the ‘Seven Sages’ of Greece. Starting with Thales, each one of the sages passed the matter on to another, with Solon eventually declaring that it should be placed in the temple of Apollo at Delphi.note golden apple A reference to ‘the apple of discord’ in classical mythology, tossed by Eris (the personification of strife) into the feast of the gods at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and triggering the conflict between Aphrodite, Athena and Hera which led to the Trojan War.note temperature of his body The balance of qualities in the whole body or in a particular bodily part, also referred to as the ‘temperament’ or ‘complexion’. An imbalance of these qualities was sometimes called a ‘distemperature’ (see the editor’s Introduction).source and the like According to Herodotus (7.35), Xerxes I of Persia (ruled 486–465 BCE) set about whipping the Hellespont (now the Dardanelles strait) in a fit of rage, after two bridges built across it by his men had been destroyed in a storm; their construction of a canal through the peninsula of Mount Athos, however, was successful.gloss rakest Scratch (or, alternatively, drag away or pull apart).gloss afternoon men Men given to drinking alcohol after lunch, or simply habitual drinkers.about Dionysus The Greek god of wine and intoxication, but also, among other things, of ritual madness and ecstasy (his Roman counterpart being Bacchus).source pauci Promethei, multi Epimethei According to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod, the name of Prometheus means ‘forethinker’ (and hence signifies forethought), and that of his brother Epimetheus means ‘afterthinker’ (signifying afterthought). In Hesiod’s account, Prometheus was a clever trickster, capable of stealing the fire of Zeus and giving it to man, but the foolish Epimetheus accepted Hephaestus’ gift of Pandora, releasing all manner of evils into the world – see also above, .about Carolus Sapiens, Philippus Bonus, Lodovicus Pius Charles V (‘the Wise’), king of France (1338–80), Philip III (‘the Good’), duke of Burgundy (1396–1467), and Louis IX (‘the Pious’), king of France (1214–70).note an aristocracy … Politicians For classical political theorists (‘Politicians’), aristocracy is the constitutional rule by ‘the best’ (usually identified as the nobility), as distinguished from monarchy and popular government or democracy.note multi Thyrsigeri, pauci Bacchi The contrast between bearers of the thyrsus (a staff tipped with an ornament like a pine cone, carried by votaries of Dionysus or Bacchus) and true mystical followers of the god is drawn by Plato in the Phaedo (69C–D).about Archytas Tarentinus Archytas of Tarentum, an ancient Greek Pythagorean philosopher (fl. c. 400–350 BCE) said to have invented mathematical mechanics.about Geber Or ‘pseudo-Geber’, the author(s) of an anonymous thirteenth-century corpus of alchemical work that includes material on alphabetical numerology, now sometimes thought to be the thirteenth-century Italian Franciscan Paul of Taranto, but formerly identified with the ninth-century Islamic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan (the real ‘Geber’).about Alkindus the Mathematician The influential Arabic philosopher, mathematician and polymath Al-Kindi (d. c. 870 CE).about Ptolemaeus The ancient Greek astronomer and polymath Claudius Ptolemaeus, or Ptolemy (c. 90–168 CE).gloss idiots Unskilled or untrained people.about Suisset the Calculator The English natural philosopher and mathematician Richard Swineshead (fl. c. 1340–54), famous as the author of the Liber calculationum.gloss deciphered Represented, portrayed.note the sacrifice of Dionysius A slightly misleading translation of ‘Dionysi sacra’ (‘the rites of Dionysus’) in the commentary on Plato’s Republic (1469) by the Italian Neoplatonist philosopher Marsilio Ficino, who claims that the Dionysian rites signified this kind of spiritual ‘drunkenness’ for Orpheus.note sacerdos Aegyptius In note ‘h’, the Egyptian priest from Plato’s Timaeus is said to have rebuked the Greeks as perpetual children.gloss issue Outcome, result.about Sorites In logic, a ‘chain’ or series of connected syllogisms, in which the predicate of one proposition is the subject of the next.about Phocion An Athenian statesman and general, and a politically conservative pupil of Plato. His opposition to democracy is related by Plutarch, and he was executed for his Macedonian sympathies in the brief democratic revolution in 318 BCE.gloss never a barrel better herring Proverbially, ‘they are all basically the same’, or ‘much of a muchness’.source Copernicus, Atlas his successor Atlas, the Titan from classical mythology tricked by Heracles (Hercules) into holding up the sky, is presented by Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 4.27.5) as the founder of astronomy.gloss in sober sadness In earnest.gloss creatures Created things, creations.about Rue A species of ruta, Ruta graveolens.source that artificial … them all At 1.1.3.3 below, Burton explains that ‘artificial’ melancholy is ‘immaterial’, and distinct from the ‘natural’ subspecies of the disease in so far as it is adventitious – that is, principally caused not by black bile but by factors external to the body. The point here is that every organism is susceptible to this ‘artificial’ kind of melancholy.gloss terse Refined, cultured.gloss uncivil Uncivilized, barbarous.about Lop and Belgian in Asia ‘Lop’ was the name given by Marco Polo to the kingdom of Charklik (now Ruoqiang in China), located near the Taklamakan Desert. ‘Belgian’ refers generally to Tartary, but also more specifically, according to the Italian cartographer Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), to the obscure promontory on the northeastern cape of Eurasia usually known as ‘Tabin’.about Alexandretta The Turkish city and district of İskenderun, sometimes known as Scanderoon.about Bantam The Javanese port city of Banten.source Pisa On the ‘bad air’ in this city, see below, p. 238 (1.2.2.5).about Durazzo The Italian name for the Albanian city of Durrës. St.about John de Ullua San Juan de Ulúa, a Spanish settlement overlooking the port of Veracruz in Mexico.about Podolians Inhabitants of Podolia, a region in what is now southwestern Ukraine.source Cremonae The phrase in note ‘a’ is a quotation from Virgil (Eclogues 9.26), which laments the land confiscations for the resettlement of military veterans after the Battle of Philippi (42 BCE), which were extended to Mantua because those from nearby Cremona were not sufficient.source Interdum … olim Mauritania, &c. Note ‘b’ probably refers to the ancient reputation of Mauretania – the territory of the Moors extending from the River Ampsaga in Numidia to the Atlantic – as a land populated by dangerous wild animals (as portrayed, for example, in Horace, Odes 1.22).gloss barred Blocked up, made inaccessible.about Brundisium The Latin name for Brindisi.source Gerar The Philistine settlement mentioned in Genesis 20:1–18, possibly in what is now the valley of Nahal Gerar in Israel.about Barcino The Latin name for Barcelona.source Achan’s fault Achan was stoned and burned for stealing some of the spoils of Jericho, which had been consecrated for the treasury of the Lord’s House; this resulted in the collective punishment of the Israelites by God (Joshua 7:1–26). His name is hence associated with greed or simony.about Sardanapalus The legendary king of Assyria said to have lived in the seventh century BCE.about Dionysius Junior Dionysius II, tyrant of Syracuse (c. 397–c. 343 BCE).about Heliogabalus The Roman emperor Elagabalus (c. 203–22 CE).about Periander Tyrant of Corinth (d. 587 BCE).about Pisistratus Tyrant of Athens (d. 527 BCE).about Tarquinius Probably Lucius Tarquinius Superbus (ruled 534–509 BCE), the last king of Rome, regarded as a tyrant and exiled – although the reference may be to the fifth king, Lucius Tarquinius Priscus (ruled 616–579 BCE), who was assassinated.about Timocrates Timocrates of Lampsacus (fourth to third century BCE), disciple-turned-opponent of Epicurus (though Timophanes, who became tyrant of Corinth in 366, is perhaps meant here).about Childericus Probably Childeric III (c. 717–c. 754 CE), king of Francia and the last of the Merovingian dynasty, who was deposed in 751 – although possibly his predecessor Childeric II (c. 653–75), who was assassinated.about Appius Claudius Appius Claudius Crassus, said to have led a tyrannical regime in the Second Decemvirate (450–449 BCE), when a board of ten magistrates with consular powers was set up to compile new laws for Rome.source Andronicus Governor of Antioch in the second century BCE, and involved with the Jewish High Priest Menelaus in the assassination of another High Priest, Onias III (2 Maccabees 4:31–8).about Galeacius Sforza Galeazzo Maria Sforza, duke of Milan (1444–76).about Alexander Medices Alessandro de’ Medici, duke of Florence (1510–37).gloss emulators Competitors, rivals.about Guelphs and Ghibellines The main rival factions in the city-states of central and northern Italy in the Middle Ages. The former supported the papacy, the latter the Holy Roman Emperor.source all his subjects The Antigonus mentioned here is Antigonus II Gonatas, king of Macedon (c. 277/6–239 BCE), whose correspondence with the Stoic philosopher Zeno is recorded by Diogenes Laertius (7.1).gloss mutine Mutiny.gloss innovations Revolutions, insurrections.about When Catiline rebelled in Rome A reference to the notorious failed conspiracy, led by the aristocratic senator Lucius Sergius Catilina (108–62 BCE) to overthrow the consulship of Cicero in 63 BCE.about Jack Cade, Tom Straw, Kett Three infamous English rebel leaders of somewhat lower (or murkier) social status: Jack Cade, of whose origins little is known, led an uprising in Kent in 1450; Jack (not Tom) Straw is a figure of some obscurity who was involved in the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 (according to some accounts it was the pseudonym of Wat Tyler or of one of the other leaders); Robert Kett, whose relatively wealthy family had once belonged to the gentry, led a revolt in Norfolk in 1549.about Geraldus Possibly the Italian lawyer Matthaeus Gribaldus (Matteo Gribaldi, d. 1564).note fori tintinabula This phrase, taken – along with others in this passage – from the third book of the Italian humanist scholar and physician Julius Caesar Scaliger’s Poetices libri septem (1561), literally translates as ‘bells of the courts’. Scaliger explains that it is an appropriate insult to throw at a soi-disant legal ‘orator’.gloss catchpoles Tax-collectors or petty officers of justice.note civilian A practitioner of Roman civil law (rather than canon or common law).gloss stale Decoy.gloss jar Discord, dispute.gloss causes Legal cases.gloss daysmen Mediators or umpires.about Alfakins or chief Judge Fuqaha, experts in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh).gloss scede Or ‘schede’, a papyrus strip.about Scytala Laconica The skytale, a secret method of communication invented by the Spartans, in which a message was first imprinted by the sender upon a thin strip of leather wound round a wooden cylinder, made illegible by detaching the strip from the cylinder, and then revealed when the recipient rewound the leather on a cylinder of equal diameter.gloss disannulled Abolished, annulled.note termers People who resorted to London during a law term, either for legal business in the courts, or for entertainment or criminality.gloss incult Uncultivated, wild.about happy reign The author of this work was the lawyer and poet Sir John Davies (c. 1569–1626), who had served under James I as Solicitor-General in Ireland since 1603.about Parks Enclosed portions of land held by royal grant or prescription, and reserved for the keeping and hunting of deer and other game.about Forests Woodland districts, typically belonging to the king, also set aside for hunting.about Quinctius in Livy The Roman statesman and general Titus Quinctius Flamininus (c. 229–174 BCE).note the fortunate Isles The Isles of the Blessed, the residence of heroes in Greek and Celtic mythology, and said to be located somewhere in the Western (Atlantic) Ocean.about two of their Captains … round about the world The circumnavigators Sir Francis Drake (1540–96) and Sir Thomas Cavendish (c. 1560–92).gloss manured Cultivated, managed.about a wise, learned, Religious King, another Numa … a true Josiah This passage was present in the first edition of 1621, when James I was on the English throne, but it remained unaltered in the later editions published after Charles I had become king in March 1625. Josiah (c. 649–609 BCE) was a king of Judah, famed, like the legendary Roman king Numa Pompilius, for his religious reforms (2 Chronicles 34–5).about Lycurgus The legendary founder and lawgiver of ancient Sparta.about Greichgea Kraichgau, a mountainous region in southwestern Germany.note 24 Italian miles over An ‘Italian mile’ varied in length, ranging between seven-eighths and one and a quarter English miles. According to the traveller and geographer Fynes Moryson, writing in 1617, an Italian mile was 1,000 paces in length (and so identical to a Roman mile), and an English one was 1,500 paces (1,760 yards).note twelve miles over by their scale A German mile was typically between four and five English miles. According to Fynes Moryson, it was ‘more than three English, or five Italian miles’.about Portugallia interamnis Literally, ‘Portugal between the rivers’: the region between the Douro and Minho Rivers.about Peru, or Nova Hispania The Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru, created in 1542, included what is now Peru but also most of the territories of South America under Spanish rule. ‘Nova Hispania’ (literally, ‘New Spain’) included Mexico and its surrounding territories but also extended into what is now the southern USA, as well as parts of South America and Oceania.note any stuff almost The source upon which this passage is loosely based, Giovanni Botero’s De illustrium statu & politia (1607), suggests that ‘stuff’ here means raw material. But the term may refer more narrowly to textile or woollen fabric, or alternatively to manufactured material.about Paulus Aemilius The Roman statesman and general Lucius Aemilius Paullus (c. 229–160 BCE), whose forces, on the orders of the senate, sacked Epirus in northwestern Greece in 167.about Mount Taygetus The highest mountain in the Taygetus range, in the Peloponnesian peninsula of southern Greece.note the Saxon Heptarchy The seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of the early Middle Ages (East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria).about Rheti Or ‘R(h)aeti’, a group of Alpine tribes, identified in antiquity as descendants of the Etruscans, and, since the Middle Ages, the inhabitants of the province of Raetia (roughly speaking the territory of modern-day Grisons).about Ragusa The Republic of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, was an independent maritime state.about Those ancient Massilians The inhabitants of the ancient Greek colony of Massalia (Massilia in Roman writers), now Marseille.about Selim the first Turkish Emperor Selim I (1470–1520), Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.about Tauris The ancient name for several places, including the region now known as Crimea and the cities of Tabriz and Hamedan in modern-day Iran. Here, however, Burton has been misled by Robert Peterson’s mistranslation of ‘Taurunum’ (the Latin name for Zemun, now part of Belgrade) in Botero’s De illustrium statu & politia.about Henry Duke of Anjou … Poland Henri of Valois (1551–89) was elected king of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1573, a year before ascending the French throne as Henri III.about James the first in Scotland James I (1394–1437), king of Scotland.gloss clothing Cloth-making.gloss Gaunt Ghent.about Arabia Petraea The name of the ‘Arabian Province’ of the Roman Empire, bordering what was then the southern frontier of Syria and the northern frontier of Egypt.about Ormus in Persia The island of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.gloss opportunity The advantage given by a suitable or accessible site.note intellectus agens The ‘agent’ or ‘active’ intellect, an essential component of the rational intelligence of the human being in Aristotelian psychology; see 1.1.2.10 below.about Mexico That is, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán (now Mexico City).about Tails Inferior or less valuable parts.gloss ploughs Means of earning a livelihood.gloss riot Debauchery, dissipation or excess.about Egyptian vagabonds The Romani people, who first came to England in the early sixteenth century, were sometimes thought to originate from Egypt – hence the name ‘Gypsies’.about Carolus Magnus Charlemagne, or ‘Charles the Great’ (742–814 CE), king of the Franks and the Lombards, and Holy Roman Emperor.source the Duke of Saxony Burton’s source, the German political theorist Henning Arnisaeus (1570–1636), refers to Augustus, elector (but not duke) of Saxony from 1553 to 1586.about Potosa in Peru Now Potosí in Bolivia, famous for its silver mines, which were discovered in 1545 and subsequently an important source of revenue for the Spanish Empire.note at Ostium The artificial enclosed harbour at Portus (two miles north of Ostia), which was linked to the River Tiber by a canal. Initially ordered by the emperor Claudius, it was built in 42–64 CE and then expanded and improved by Trajan in 103.about Dioclesiani Therma The Baths of Diocletian, built in 298–306 CE.about Fucinus Lacus The Fucine lake (Laco Fucino) had been partially drained by Claudius over a period of eleven years, according to Suetonius (The Deified Claudius 20).note that Piraeus in Athens The Athenian politician and general Themistocles began the development and fortification of the port at Piraeus in 493/2 BCE.about Civitas Philippi Philippi, now Filippoi in northeastern Greece.about Heraclea in Thrace Formerly Perinthus, now Marmara Ereğlisi in Turkey.note those Appian and Flaminian ways The Via Appia and the Via Flaminia, two important Roman roads built in the republican period, and connecting Rome to Brundisium (Brindisi) and Arminium (Rimini) respectively.source Moeris and Sesostris According to Herodotus, the artificial ‘Lake of Moeris’ was named after the Egyptian pharaoh responsible for its construction. He probably had Amenemhet III (who ruled c. 1860–c. 1814 BCE) in mind, but this is a mistake possibly deriving from a misunderstanding of the Egyptian term for ‘canal’ (mi-wer). Sesostris was a legendary Egyptian king whose achievements, based on those of three pharaohs of the Twelfth Dynasty named Senusret, are recorded by Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus.about Amasis Aegypti Rex Note ‘d’ refers to the pharaoh Amasis II, who reigned 570–525 BCE.note corrivations of Waters Confluences of streams, but here apparently referring to irrigation channels.gloss Moors Marshes.about Masinissa King of Numidia (238–148 BCE).gloss battable Fertile in pasture.note in Egypt, about Babylon and Damascus ‘Babylon’ here is the city now known as Cairo; Damascus was a provincial capital of the Mamluk Empire, ruled by the Sultan of Egypt, between 1260 and 1516 (Burton is here drawing on an account first published in 1510 by the Italian travel writer Ludovico di Varthema).note cubits A cubit was an ancient measurement of length deriving from the forearm, usually about eighteen to twenty-two inches.about Ptolemy The Egyptian ruler Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE).gloss absolved Completed.about Demetrius Demetrius I Poliorcetes of Macedon (336–283 BCE), whose plans for a canal were never implemented.about Herodes Atticus Tiberius Claudius Atticus Herodes (c. 101–77 CE), a wealthy Athenian sophist and benefactor of Greek cities.note our Picts’ wall Hadrian’s Wall, setting what was then the northern limit of the Roman Empire in the province of Britannia, and beyond which lay the territory of the Picts.about Schoenunte Schoinous (Kalamaki) on the Saronic Gulf, east of Corinth.about which Amurath the Turk demolished The Hexamilion (‘six-mile’) wall was reportedly destroyed in 1446 by the forces of Sultan Murad II (1404–51).about Rhodanus The River Rhône.source from Arar to Mossella From the River Saône to the Moselle River.about Aurelianus The Roman emperor Aurelian (Lucius Domitius Aurelianus), who ruled 270–75 CE.note some Indian plants That is, plants (such as potatoes) from the West Indies.gloss salt Via the ‘gabelle’, a tax on salt.about Durius The Douro.about Hebrus The Maritsa.about Bishop Atwater William Atwater (1440–1521), bishop of Lincoln.gloss vent and utterance Opportunity for the selling or bartering of goods.about Aulis Now Avlida.about Ambracia Now Arta.about Sus Minervam An abbreviation of ‘Sus Minervam docet’, an ancient proverb deriding the attempt of a stupid person to instruct a wise one.note verjuice and oatmeal is good for a Parrot A comical homophonic translation of ‘veritas odium parit’ that plays on the sourness of verjuice.gloss general visitor A visiting inspector-general.about Rosy Cross men The mystical Rosicrucian fraternity: a fictitious secret society, identified in the seventeenth century and allegedly devoted to mysticism and alchemy, for which two anonymous manifestos, the Fama fraternitatis Rosae Crucis and the Confessio fraternitatis, had been published in 1614 and 1615.gloss policy Civil order, polity.note as he did Hesione Scenes from the life of Heracles (Hercules) in classical mythology: his defeat of the shape-shifting river-god Achelous, a rival suitor for Deianira – on whom, see below, ; his fifth labour, to clean the stables of King Augeas in a single day; his killing of two tyrants, the Thracian king Diomedes, who owned a team of man-eating mares which were kept supplied with human victims (during his eighth labour), and the Egyptian king Busiris, who habitually slaughtered foreigners entering Egypt (during his eleventh labour); his killing of the giant Cacus and the robber Lacinius after they had stolen from him some of the cattle he had been sent to obtain from the giant Geryon (his tenth labour); and his rescue of the Trojan princess Hesione from a sea-monster sent by Poseidon (Neptune).gloss vindicate Rescue, or liberate.note the Torrid Zone The region situated between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, in which the sun is directly overhead on at least one occasion during the year; see also below, .source Theban Crates The Cynic philosopher Crates of Thebes (c. 365–c. 285 BCE), who, according to Diogenes Laertius (6.5), lived in virtuous poverty after giving away his large personal fortune to his fellow citizens.note those mighty Maeotian fens The marshlands lying northeast of the Sea of Azov (Lake Maeotis in antiquity), which adjoins the Black Sea.about Hercynian woods The Hercynian Forest, which stretched across southern Germany in antiquity.about Scorbutum, Plica, morbus Neapolitanus The epidemical diseases of scurvy, trichoma (or ‘Polish plait’) and syphilis (first identified in Naples, hence morbus Neapolitanus – though it was also known as morbus Gallicus, ‘the French disease’ or ‘French pox’; see below, 1.1.1.2).about Licinius Actually ‘Lycinus’, the character who ridicules the ambitions of Timolaus at the end of Lucian’s dialogue The Ship.note by Commissioners Boccalini’s Ragguagli di Parnaso (1612/13), one of whose English translators was Burton’s acquaintance William Vaughan – on whom, see below, . It imagines a custom in which Apollo presents princes and potentates with the disorders in their commonwealths, and then challenges them either to defend themselves from criticism or else to implement reforms. The god subsequently appoints the ‘Seven Sages’ of Greece, along with Cato and Seneca, as commissioners to effect a ‘general Reformation’ of the world.source lapis super lapidem sedeat Probably an adaptation of Christ’s prediction of the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem in Matthew 24:2 (‘non relinquetur hic lapis super lapidem qui non destruatur’: ‘there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone that shall not be destroyed’), suggesting persistence rather than removal.about Mare del Zur The Pacific Ocean (after its Spanish name, ‘Mar del Zur’).note the Cyanean Isles in the Euxine sea The Symplegades (‘Clashing Rocks’) in the Bosporus strait, which in Greek mythology were said to move around randomly, being unattached to the sea bed, and were successfully navigated by Jason and the Argonauts. The ‘Euxine’ is the Greek name for the Black Sea.gloss coasts Regions, places or countries.note these presents The conventional opening words of a legal proclamation or charter; the phrase ‘these presents’ refers to the present document or its contents.note so much money … for casting a Nativity That is, a very substantial amount. In his De interrogationibus libellus (1555), the Italian polymath and physician Girolamo Cardano warns astrologers not to accept small fees, and says that he once rejected the offer of 200 crowns for drawing up a single horoscope.note advowsons ‘Advowson’ is the exclusive right in ecclesiastical law to present a member of the clergy to a benefice, or more generally to patronage of a church or religious house.about Staples A town or place granted the right of purchase of certain classes of export goods by royal authority.about Hippodamus Milesius In note ‘e’, Hippodamus of Miletus (b. c. 500 BCE), was the most famous town-planner in ancient Greece.about Rhegium Lepidi Now Reggio Emilia in northern Italy, built within hexagonal town walls.about Cambalu A corruption of ‘Khanbaliq’, which had been the capital of the Mongol Empire since the reign of Kublai Khan (1260–94), and now Beijing.about Palma Palmanova, a Venetian settlement in northeastern Italy, built as a fortress in the shape of a nine-pointed star and founded in 1593.gloss baser Lower in height.note after the latest manner of fortification Complex geometrical arrangements of ditches, moats and projecting bastions made of earth, designed to withstand gunfire.gloss burses Or ‘bourses’, commercial exchanges.gloss artillery gardens Practice grounds for artillery.gloss gymnics Gymnastics.gloss hospitals Charitable institutions, or asylums, for the poor, infirm or aged.gloss pest-houses Hospitals for those suffering from infectious disease, especially plague.gloss a satisfactory almshouse An almshouse providing
