‘satisfaction’ or atonement for sin.gloss benevolences Voluntary gifts of money.gloss donaries Donations or votive offerings.about Misnia Meissen in eastern Germany.about Stetein in Pomerland Szczecin (formerly German Stettin), the capital city of the Polish province of West Pomerania.about Labedum in Ionia Lebedus, which in Roman times hosted gatherings of Ionian actors and festivals dedicated to Bacchus (Dionysus).note pendant Modern editors have sometimes emended this to ‘pedant’, but in the seventeenth century the term ‘pendant’ could refer to a testicle, and the comical sense of a ‘hanger-on’ may be intended here.about Aediles, Quaestors Magistrates in the Roman Republic responsible, respectively, for the maintenance of public buildings and festivals, and for the management of public finances.gloss pupils Orphans who are minors, and consequently, in civil law, wards.gloss all public houses Communal buildings of all kinds (rather than all taverns).about Mr. Carew … doth raise, &c. Note ‘c’ refers to discussions about enclosure, which had traditionally been associated with depopulation and the impoverishment of the labouring poor. ‘Cotswold’ refers to the finer wool of sheep from the Cotswolds; Burton’s source, the Cornish antiquary Richard Carew (1555–1620), simply says that after enclosure, ‘Cornish Sheep come but little behind the Eastern flocks’ – that is, those found in counties east of Cornwall.note fine In feudal society, the fee paid by a tenant or vassal to a landlord on some alteration of the tenancy.about Fellmongers Dealers in animal skins or hides.gloss Chandlers Candle-sellers.gloss curriers Leather dressers and colourers.gloss subordinate as the other Subordinate, that is, to the power of the king, as in civil law.gloss impropriations Annexations of benefices (or their revenues) to a lay corporation or lay proprietor.gloss common societies Shared associations, such as guilds, corporations or charitable foundations.note the literati in China The ‘learned class’ of China, cultured intellectuals who were employed as officials in the Chinese state bureaucracy from the seventeenth to the early twentieth century.about Auditors People who listen to sermons, or receive spiritual instruction orally.gloss delegacy A body or committee of delegates.gloss to depend To be suspended, await determination.about Solon’s Areopagites The Athenian council of the Areopagus, according to the Athenian Constitution (a work often attributed to Aristotle), was instituted by Solon in the early sixth century BCE to act as the guardian of the laws and overseer of the activities of magistrates.gloss proling Prowling.gloss diapason Complete agreement, concord.gloss jument Beast of burden.gloss merry-meetings Festivities, convivial gatherings.note that Saccarum festum … Saturnals in Rome Two ancient festivals in which social norms were overturned, and thereby associated with licentious behaviour: the Persian Sacaea, possibly adopted from the Babylonian New Year Festival, and the Roman Saturnalia, a carnivalesque celebration that took place in December.source En leges ipsi Veneri Martique timendas The allusion to Mars and Venus in note ‘e’, which is a quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.31), refers to their adultery – see below, .source a woman at 30 In note ‘i’, the ages given are incorrect; and, from the second edition of 1624 onwards – where ‘30’ was replaced by ‘20’ – also confusing, as this brought Burton into line with the guidelines in Plato’s Republic (460E). Aristotle, in fact, states in the Politics (7.14) that men should be thirty-seven and women eighteen before they marry.gloss enormous Abnormal or extraordinary.gloss intempestive Inopportune, untimely.note anno 1621 In note ‘b’, the author of the Tract against the High Rate of Usury, which had been presented to parliament in 1621 and published anonymously in 1623, was Sir Thomas Culpeper (1577/8–1662).note multiplicity of offices, of supplying by deputies The same person holding two or more offices or positions, especially ecclesiastical ones (also called ‘pluralism’), and appointing a deputy to discharge duties on his behalf. Burton added this restriction in the second edition of 1624 (the year in which his income from the benefice of Walesby was added to that from Osney).note those rectified by the Primum mobile … resolve bodies by Algebra, Stereometry The process of correctly calculating and determining (‘rectifying’ and ‘resolving’) the measurements of three-dimensional objects by astronomical and geometrical methods: the primum mobile (‘prime mover’) is the outermost celestial sphere – see below, – revolving around the earth in a twenty-four-hour cycle; a ‘geometrical pace’ is the distance between successive stationary positions of the same foot when walking (roughly a length of five feet); ‘stereometry’ is the art or science of measuring solid bodies. Burton’s interest in this area is perhaps related to his earlier service as Clerk of the Market at Oxford (see the editor’s Introduction).about not Minucius Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus Cunctator (the ‘Delayer’, d. 203 BCE), the Roman general renowned for his struggle with Hannibal in the Second Punic War with Carthage (218–201), and responsible for the famous ‘Fabian’ strategy of refusing to engage with the enemy except when absolutely necessary; Marcus Minucius Rufus (d. 216), second in command to Fabius and also his political opponent, rejected the strategy by engaging Hannibal’s army at Geronium in 217, and subsequently had to be rescued by his more cautious superior.gloss defalcations Deductions.gloss reparations Repairs.gloss included Confined.gloss corsives Sources of care or annoyance.about Economical body Household (from the Greek οἶκος, ‘house’).note as Actaeon was by his hounds In the oldest version of the classical myth, Zeus (Jupiter) punishes the hero Actaeon for raping Semele by sending Artemis (Diana) to turn him into a stag and set his own dogs on him. In other versions, his offence is to boast that he is a better hunter than Artemis, or to see the goddess naked while she is bathing, or to try to marry her in her own sanctuary.source But of this elsewhere See 1.2.3.10 and 1.2.4.6 below.gloss naught Morally bad.gloss liquorish Greedy or lecherous.gloss quean Prostitute.gloss soft Simple-minded, lacking ordinary intelligence or common sense.note the Thrush and the Swallow in Aesop In Aesop’s fable ‘Of the Thrush Entering into Friendship with the Swallow’, the thrush, who prefers a cold climate, is told he is incompatible with the swallow, who prefers a warm one.gloss compellations Names, titles, or words by which someone is addressed.gloss daughter-in-law Possibly, stepdaughter (a now obsolete meaning).gloss descend to their present fortunes That is, deign to stoop, or condescend, to their deteriorated circumstances.gloss when they concur In note ‘e’, ‘concur’ means ‘coincide’ or, more specifically here, ‘collide’.gloss casualties Precarious accidents or uncertainties.gloss drenched Drowned, overwhelmed.gloss secure Free from worry, put at ease.about Hieron The Sicilian tyrant Hieron I of Syracuse (ruled 478–466 BCE).about Simonides The poet Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BCE).note take it up Valerius Maximus (7.ext.5) attributes this saying, actually addressed to a diadem not a robe, to an anonymous king. Elsewhere, Stobaeus identifies him as Antigonus, without stating which of the Macedonian kings with this name is meant.note the nearer the worse As Erasmus explains in the 1526 edition of his Adagia, the proverb warns against involvement with the very powerful.note casting Counters Counters used to assist calculation or reckoning up, particularly in book-keeping (the process of ‘casting accounts’).about Obs and Sols Objections and Solutions, part of the scholastic disputational method employed in Renaissance theology.about School divinity Scholastic theology, as taught in the universities.gloss intricable Entangling, perplexing.about Wit whither wilt In note ‘b’, a proverbial phrase addressed to someone whose tongue (or ‘wit’) is running away with him.source one calls it Cicero, in On Divination (2.43.90).about Resolutus The nickname of the philosopher and theologian John Baconthorpe (c. 1290–1345/52).about Doctor Seraphicus The title given to St Bonaventure (1221–74).note cere-diminuit-brum An adaptation of a jocular tmesis (word-splitting), traditionally attributed to Ennius, ‘saxo cere comminuit brum’ (‘he split the brain with a rock’), which splits the term for brain (‘cerebrum’) with the word ‘splits’ (‘comminuit’).gloss circumvents Captures, entraps.gloss glozing Cajoling, coaxing or representing speciously.note and who doth not The classical notion of mad poetic ‘fury’ or ‘frenzy’, the divine rapture experienced by poets while composing their works, was much discussed in the Renaissance.note Si furor sit Lyaeus … & Poeta, &c. The sense of the partial Latin quotation in note ‘e’, which is adapted from the Anacreontica (1554) by Julius Caesar Scaliger, is clarified by the original: ‘Si furor est Cupido,/Si furor est Lyaeus, Si furor est Thalia,/Quoties furor, furor, furor/Amans, bibens, poeta?’ (‘If madness is Cupid,/If madness is Bacchus,/If madness is Thalia,/How often do I become mad, mad, mad/In loving, drinking, {being} a poet?’) ‘Thalia’ is the Muse of comedy and idyllic poetry.gloss beray Befoul.note humble-bees, dors or beetles ‘Humble-bee’ was another name for the bumble-bee; ‘dor’ could refer to the bumble-bee, but also to the hornet or several different species of flying insect, including the dung beetle or may-bug.gloss castigations Emendations.about Artists Here, scholars or philosophers, or more specifically those skilled in one of the seven ‘liberal arts’.about besieged Archimedes of Syracuse (287–212 BCE) died when the city was captured by the Romans. In a story related by Plutarch, he was killed by a Roman soldier because he refused to stop contemplating one of his mathematical diagrams.gloss combustion Commotion, tumult.note They get their wisdom by eating Piecrust some In note ‘g’, the saying is a version of the proverb ‘Pie lid makes people wise’. Here, the ironic implication is apparently that a full stomach encourages the expression of (unwise) opinions. Traditionally, the saying refers to the removal of the pie lid – which served primarily to protect the pie filling from vermin and insects – as the means by which a person became ‘wise’ as to the contents of the pie.about Semiramis The beautiful, mythical queen of Assyria whose great achievements and dissolute lifestyle were the subject of many ancient, medieval and Renaissance anecdotes. Her legend is evidently based on the historical figure of Sammu-Ramat, the wife of the Assyrian king Shamshi-Adad V (824–811 BCE).about in him Machiavelli actually says this, in the Istorie fiorentine (1532), about Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–92) rather than his grandfather Cosimo (1389–1464).about like water Richard, first earl of Cornwall and king of Germany (1209–72), bribed the imperial electors, but having failed to obtain the support of the papacy he was never crowned Holy Roman Emperor.note horn-mad Originally, with reference to horned beasts, so enraged as to be ready to gore someone with one’s horn (and hence, mad with anger). There is also an allusion to sexual jealousy here, since cuckolds were sometimes said to wear horns on their brows – an idea that may originate in the archaic practice of removing the comb from a castrated cock and grafting its spurs on to the root, which then grew into horns.about Signior Deliro A character in Ben Jonson’s Every Man out of His Humour (1599), described as ‘a fellow sincerely besotted on his own wife’, called Fallace, ‘& so rapt with a conceit of her perfections, that he simply holds himself unworthy of her’.about Hercules Furens, Maenades, and Corybantes Classical exempla of insane frenzy: ‘Raging Hercules’ – see below, ; the female worshippers of Dionysus (Bacchus), whose rituals involved ecstatic frenzy; and the semi-divine priests who worship in the orgiastic cults of Dionysus and Cybele with noisy flute music and wild dancing.source Deucalion and Pyrrha’s stones The stones cast after the great flood, which had been unleashed by Zeus (Jupiter) as punishment for human hubris, by the hero Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha. In Ovid’s Metamorphoses (1.313–47), the stones were said to be transformed gradually into men and women, thereby repopulating the earth. Famian.about Strada de bajulis … semisculptis Note ‘c’ refers to an anecdote told about a fountain on the Via Lata in Rome by the Italian historian Famiano Strada (1572–1649), who observed that its statue of a porter pouring water from a wine-jar was indistinguishable from the real porters who would idly gather around it.note that enchanted horn of Astolpho … themselves In Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (1532), Duke Astolfo has a magic horn that causes his enemies to flee in fright.source & laurus insana … insania affecit In note ‘d’, the ‘laurus insana’ is a species of laurel, said by Pliny the Elder (16.89) to have grown on the tomb of Amycus, the mythical king of the Bebryces in Bithynia: when taken on board a ship, its branches would induce discord and quarrelling among the crew.note the mad haven … of Daphnis insana The port of Daphne on the Black Sea, reportedly named after a large laurel grove nearby (‘Daphne’ means laurel in Greek), and called ‘insana’ through association with the ‘laurus insana’.gloss dementate Dement, drive out of one’s mind.about Midsummer moon The full moon at the time of midsummer, both of which were traditionally associated with madness.note the Dog days last all the year long In ancient astrology, the ‘Dog Star’ (Sirius) was thought to induce disease, and it was also traditionally thought to cause madness in dogs. The ‘dog days’ were the hottest part of the summer, when the Dog Star was rising.gloss sand-blind Half-blind, dim-sighted.note bored Trepanned – that is, have a hole bored into the skull to provoke the escape of pathogenic vapours; see 2.5.1.4 below.gloss Theologues Theologians.about Artists Here, practitioners of magical arts or occult sciences, particularly astrologers and alchemists. of whom St.about Bridget … have prophesied The mystic and saint Bridget of Sweden (1303–73), the Italian theologian Joachim of Fiore (1135–1202) and the German astrologer Johannes Liechtenberger (d. 1503) were seen by some to have foretold the Rosicrucian movement.about Elias artifex their Theophrastian master The occult philosopher, physician and visionary Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541) was said to have predicted that he would be succeeded by ‘Elias Artifex’ (‘Elias the Artist’, named after the wandering prophet Elijah), a mythical figure who would renovate the arts and sciences.about Ammonius the philosopher The Platonist philosopher Ammonius Saccas is famous mainly for his teaching of Plotinus at Alexandria in 232–42 CE, but he is also sometimes identified as the teacher of Origen, the Christian Father.source Sapientium Octavus An ironic remark taken from the Satires (2.296) of Horace; see above, .about Lorarios The lorarius was an ancient Roman official whose job was to flog slaves.about Rabelais … Physician The French satirist François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553) was also a medical doctor.gloss dry Miserly, stingy.gloss heteroclites Abnormal or eccentric people.gloss ordinary Occurring in the course of regular, everyday life; customary.gloss winch Wince.gloss salve Heal.about Dionysian feasts The festivals of Dionysus in Athens took place in the winter months, and started with the rural Dionysia, which involved performances of comedies, tragedies and dithyrambs. Here, in conjunction with the Roman Saturnalia – see above, – and the comments about leisured idleness and freedom of speech, they carry the implication of carnivalesque comic licence.note as he said … periculum est The Dutch poet and scholar Daniel Heinsius, in an address to the reader printed in the fourth edition of his Poemata (1613).about Vacunal fires Vacuna was the ancient Roman goddess of the countryside, to whom sacrifices were made by rural worshippers after the harvest had been gathered – hence her association with leisure.about Οὔτις ἔλεγεν The Greek name derives from the ninth book of the Odyssey, where Odysseus pretends to be called Οὔτις (‘Nobody’) in order to trick the Cyclops Polyphemus. Burton’s immediate source, however, is the Nemo (1510) of the German scholar, poet and satirist Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), which has been explicitly quoted above, at p. 120.note turn the buckle of his girdle Proverbially, ‘get ready to fight’: a saying that derives from wrestling, in which the combatants would turn the buckles of their girdles behind them before engaging.about Pontus In note ‘b’, the Senecan reference is to the ancient region on the south coast of the Black Sea, which had been the heartland of a Persian satrapy, and then a kingdom, before it became a Roman province.source nec dum finitus Orestes This phrase from Juvenal (Satires 1.6) originally refers to an incomplete literary composition, but here it signifies the persistent raving of a madman. In Greek mythology, Orestes was driven mad and tormented relentlessly by the Furies after killing his mother Clytemnestra, who had murdered his father Agamemnon with the aid of her lover Aegisthus.gloss have and hold Tenaciousness.about Thomas’ Shrine The shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. · about Paxes Precious tablets, depicting the crucifixion or another holy scene, which are kissed by the celebrating priest and then the other participants at mass. · gloss cringes Acts of bowing in a servile or sycophantic manner. · gloss knocking Beating one’s breast.note tasteless The Latin adjective insulsus means both ‘tasteless’ and ‘absurd’ or ‘foolish’.about Sicilian Evensongs The ‘Sicilian Vespers’, the successful and very bloody rebellion, in 1282, against the rule of the Angevins in Sicily. · about the Duke of Alva’s tyrannies Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, the third duke of Alva (or Alba) (1507–82) was the notoriously harsh governor in the Netherlands during the early stages of the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule (1568–1648). · note those ten persecutions The persecutions of Christians carried out by the Roman emperors from Nero to Diocletian (64–311 CE).about Hours The classical Horae, goddesses of the seasons.note he makes Galen fimbriam Hippocratis Literally, ‘the fringe’ or ‘hem’ of Hippocrates (fimbrias could refer to the border or hem of a cloak, gown or robe, or to tassels hanging from it). The implication – also carried here by the term ‘skirt’, which refers to the lower part of a hanging garment – is that Galen’s works are to be regarded as the ornamental bordering of those of Hippocrates, or simply as their appendage.gloss engrossings The purchase of land (or other goods) in order to gain a monopoly.about Gotham parish The English village of Gotham, in Nottinghamshire, was traditionally labelled the home of stupid people.
